articles.title: The scene inside the National caucus room
articles.description:
National MPs are in the caucus room determining things like the leadership of New Zealand. In the absence of any information emerging from that meeting, we have taken the obvious path, and made it up. 

Here is the latest. 

There is a nervous energy in the National caucus room. Christopher Luxon has just finished up an anecdote about Chicago and is now on to Canada. 

Chris Bishop is circling the perimeter of the caucus room on a Lime scooter. 

Simeon Brown is curled up in the corner shivering, surrounded by empty packets of pseudoephedrine.

Erica Stanford is rummaging through a large duffel bag. It looks like Murray McCully is in there. 

Christopher Luxon has taken to his feet and declared – no ifs, buts or maybes – that Stuart Nash will have no place in a cabinet he leads. 

Winston Peters is not present and yet everywhere, manifest in every atom in the room. 

Christopher Luxon is on his feet reading a rousing speech from his telephone, with the peroration: “We didn’t come this far to stop now. Stand up. Hold the line. Let’s finish what we started. Would you like me to provide another version of the speech, this time with a more conciliatory tone?”

Some backbencher or other has launched into a lengthy summary of the state of play. “We knew Chris could beat Chris,” she says. “But can Chris beat Chris? If we go with Chris then Chris will shake in his boots but if we choose Chris will only make Chris feel stronger.”

Nicola Grigg says Erica Stanford is her friend but she is not a prime minister. That sparks a heated debate about who exactly is the prime minister. After a quick show of hands, John Key comes out narrowly ahead of Mike Hosking and Winston Peters.

The backbencher is still going. “And by the way how dare Chris come in here and say Chris is any better than Chris or Chris? As for Erica, well, I agree with Chris.”

Stuart Smith has been spotted curled up in a cavity above the ceiling. 

Simeon Brown is making a powerful case for Christopher Luxon, or at least he seems to be. No one can quite make out what he is saying from under the three layers of PPE.

Gerry Brownlee appears to be in great pain. Under the caucus table he is tightening a precision woodworking vice around his own fingers, “to take my mind off it all”.

Christopher Luxon has just announced he will hold a referendum on the flag. And the anthem. And also a referendum on earthquakes, good or bad?

Nicola Willis is delivering an update on the fuel stock details, detailing the supply in-country, within New Zealand waters and beyond. No one is listening. All anyone can hear is Simeon Brown groaning as his other sinus goes.

Chris Penk has 3D-printed a fixed-wing drone, armed it with a specialised anti-armour payload and sent it buzzing around the room, right behind Bishop on the Lime. Luxon is following in turn, singing ‘Bills’ by LunchMoney Lewis and chanting, mantra-like, I don’t know how to be any clearer, guys.

Christopher Luxon has just ruled out going into coalition with the National Party.

Mark Mitchell catches the drone in his teeth, chews for a minute, spits it out and grinds it into the carpet beneath his cowboy boot. 

Christopher Luxon has the Uber app open. He is scrolling furiously searching for the NZDF King Air 350 option. 

Darkness has come. Thomas Coughlan is typing.

articles.title: Will Luxon’s leadership survive the day?
articles.description:
At 9.30am National is holding an emergency caucus meeting to “resolve the issue” of Luxon’s leadership of the party (and the country), writes Henry Oliver in today’s excerpt from The Bulletin.

To receive The Bulletin in full each weekday, sign up here.

If you missed literally all the news yesterday afternoon and evening, at 9.30 this morning National is holding an emergency caucus meeting in parliament to, in the prime minister’s words, “resolve the issue” of his leadership of the party. He probably hopes that means a confirmation of support for his leadership. His rivals in the party probably hope that means one of them walks out of parliament as the 43rd prime minister of New Zealand.

How did we get here?

Depending who you ask, this has been building for a fortnight, or for the better part of a year. Yesterday afternoon, The Spinoff’s editor Veronica Schmidt summarised a brutal run (also here on At Large with Toby Manhire if you’re more of an audio-visual learner): Luxon hazily ruled out any coalition with the Opportunity Party, was forced into an apology after appearing to lecture small business owners in Rotorua, called his own foreign minister’s comments “racist” yet refused to sack him, and then, quite casually on talkback radio, committed National to an MMP referendum that blindsided his own caucus.

Monday night’s Herald story was the spark that lit the fuse this time, with one anonymous MP telling political editor Thomas Coughlan: “There’s going to be change in the top job. It’s just a question of who is going to be it.” By yesterday afternoon, 1News reported senior National MPs were weighing up whether to go to Luxon directly and tell him it was time to resign, with several senior ministers – including Erica Stanford and Simon Watts – conspicuously refusing to back him when asked. Luxon called the emergency meeting himself that evening, posting that “division and disunity” three months from the election was unfair to voters and needed resolving quickly.

It’s the second time in four months he’s faced this exact scenario. He survived an April confidence vote by a margin The Post has reported as 27 to 22, though it says a rival outlet has put it at 28 to 21 – either way, uncomfortably close.

Who’s in the running?

The name that comes up most is education minister Erica Stanford, who The Post’s Nick James notes has been touted for months due to her strong ministerial performance and popularity outside parliament (she pointedly declined to confirm either her ambitions or her confidence in Luxon when hounded by media at Auckland Airport last night). Newsroom’s Sam Sachdeva rates her chances too, noting she could be National’s answer to Jacinda Ardern’s 2017 surge, though, as the Herald’s Audrey Young reported last year, she is “more popular outside the caucus than inside it” and “is not considered a team player”. According to reporting from the Herald this morning, MP Chris Penk has been “engaging National MPs to see whether she could have the numbers”.

Chris Bishop is the other frontrunner, holding housing, transport, infrastructure and RMA reform, with well-honed political experience from his time advising Gerry Brownlee and Steven Joyce. He publicly supported Luxon yesterday, but Sachdeva notes he’s long been rumoured as an internal agitator for change, which cuts both ways – as the saying goes, “the person who wields the knife never wears the crown.”

Mark Mitchell, Nicola Willis and Simeon Brown round out the list; Willis has the finance credentials but is arguably too close to Luxon’s own record to offer a clean reset, while Brown, at 35, would become the youngest New Zealand prime minister ever. The Herald’s Coughlan reported a proposed unity ticket of Stanford as leader, Mitchell as deputy and Bishop as finance minister had been discussed, though sources stressed nothing was locked in.

What else do we know?

Not much. Yet. Willis and Bishop have both said publicly they have confidence in Luxon; so have Mark Mitchell, Matt Doocey and National’s president Sylvia Wood. But as of Tuesday night, a striking number of senior figures – not just Stanford, but Louise Upston, Paul Goldsmith, Chris Penk and Simon Watts – hadn’t given anything on the record. Former PM Sir John Key was reported to be working the phones on Luxon’s behalf, though Key told the Herald that was “untrue.”

The Spinoff’s Lyric Waiwiri-Smith gathered a range of outside views on whether a change even makes sense this close to an election. Commentator Jacqui van der Kaay framed it as weighing the risk of keeping an unpopular leader against the risk of a messy, unpredictable changeover, while PR consultant David Cormack warned that rolling Luxon risks destabilising the coalition entirely if NZ First’s Winston Peters decides to “pull the pin” in response. Former National MP Claudette Hauiti was blunter, arguing the party should have moved yesterday.

NZ First strategists told The Post’s Anneke Smith a leadership change “would not necessarily be the end of the coalition,” while ACT’s David Seymour dismissed the whole saga as a distraction from what actually matters: “We’re talking about people and the country needs policy and principles.”

What happens next?

We wait and see. And refresh our browsers constantly. On The Spinoff right now, we already have Toby Manhire and Alice Neville on the tools, liveblogging the whole thing. They’ll keep you up to date with all the news, gossip, innuendo, tea-leaf reading, until the prime minister (whoever that may be) walks out to meet the sleep-deprived-and-highly-caffeinated press gallery and claims victory, party unity, and every confidence for getting back to the basics of trying to win November’s election.

articles.title: NZX 50 dips as RBA warns on inflation
articles.description:
The New Zealand dollar gained against its trans-Tasman counterpart as the Reserve Bank of Australia kept its cash rate unchanged, while warning it was ready to hike if it needed to rein in elevated inflation.

New Zealand’s S&P/NZX 50 index slipped further into the red after the RBA’s decision, with energy heavyweights Mercury NZ and Meridian Energy the major drags on the benchmark index.

Meanwhile, newly appointed Financial Markets Authority chair James Miller will step down from the boards of Ryman Healthcare and Vista Group International once replacement directors are in place to make sure he has the bandwidth for his new role at the regulator.

And after local trading ended, Craigs Investment Partners and Barrenjoey Capital Partners confirmed the rumours, with the Australian investment bank taking on various capital markets and corporate finance staff, including Justin Queale who takes on the role of executive chair of Barrenjoey NZ.

Familiar fears

The NZX 50 dipped 27.58 points, or 0.2%, to 13,860.66, with 24 stocks declining, 22 gaining and four unchanged. The S&P/NZX 20 index futures contract for September nudged up 0.1% to 7,777 with 25 lots traded for a value of $194,000, while the NZX 20 dropped 0.3% to 7,809.34.

Turnover across the main board was $124.5 million, of which Contact Energy accounted for $14.9 million as the power company rose 0.8% to $9.04, recovering some of Monday’s decline when it reported its annual result.

Forsyth Barr analysts Andrew Harvey-Green and Hugh Lockwood kept their ‘outperform’ rating on the power company and raised their target price by 20 cents to $11.10, with the data centre joint venture with Infratil’s CDC seen as credible path to extract maximum value from Contact’s Stratford site in Taranaki.

“While it is a step away from generating and retailing electricity, it is a lower-risk approach than the one taken by Mercury,” the analysts said in a note to clients. “A JV structure, supported by project financing, will also limit Contact’s upfront capital commitment.”

Meridian fell 1.1% to $5.57 and Mercury declined 1.7% to $6.57, while lines company Vector dropped 2% to $4.88. Infratil slid 1.1% to $15.11.

The local market was softer on the day as the RBA kept its cash rate at 4.35%, while noting the pace of inflation across the Tasman remained elevated and that it would take the necessary steps to rein in consumer prices.

The kiwi dollar climbed to 83.59 Australian cents at 5pm in Auckland from 83.37 cents yesterday, while Australia’s S&P/ASX 200 index was up 0.4% in late trading.

Magellan Financial Group jumped 4.6% to five-week high A$11.01 after Barrenjoey and Craigs confirmed speculation this week of a tie-up between the trans-Tasman firms. Barrenjoey will take on Craigs staff from its corporate finance, financial markets and support roles, and provide ongoing research, trading and execution for the $40 billion of client funds overseen by Craigs’ expanding wealth business.

Stock market operator NZX rose 1% to $1.495.

Focusing the workload

Meanwhile, Ryman slipped 1.9% to $2.06 and Vista advanced 0.8% to $2.66 as FMA chair James Miller said he planned to step down from those boards to devote enough time to his new regulatory role, leaving each board once replacements have been found. Channel Infrastructure, which he chairs, slipped 2.4% to $3.27 and Fletcher Building, where he’s deputy chair, rose 2.2% to $3.79.

Gentrack rose 1.4% to $3.70 after announcing a shake-up of the board, including Spark New Zealand’s chief financial officer Stewart Taylor coming in to chair the audit and risk committee, replacing Fiona Oliver who departs at the end of the week.

Tourism Holdings posted the steepest decline on the NZX 50, falling 2.4% to $2.85, while Serko recorded the biggest gain on the day, up 2.3% at $1.75 – its 10th straight gain.

Outside the benchmark index, PGG Wrightson dropped 6.3% to $2.23, snapping a five-day rally after reporting a 16% increase in annual operating earnings and lifting its final dividend.

Millennium & Copthorne Hotels New Zealand gained 2.9% to $3.20 after the hotel operator reported a 58% jump in first-half profit, as Queenstown remained a popular destination.

The kiwi dollar traded at 58.92 US cents at 5pm from 58.86 cents yesterday, while the yield on the 10-year government bond rose 1 basis point to 4.69%, below the 4.71% on its US equivalent.

Prime Minister Christopher Luxon will hold an emergency in-person meeting with his National party caucus on Wednesday morning after the latest round of leaks questioning his leadership.

Reporting by Paul McBeth.

articles.title: Weighing the risks and rewards of rolling Christopher Luxon
articles.description:
National Party MPs will have one question as they head to an urgent caucus meeting about Christopher Luxon’s leadership today: is rolling a sitting prime minister really a viable option three months out from the election?

This scene is starting to feel like déjà vu. The setting: the National Party caucus room. The players: agitated MPs of whom some, if reports are to be believed, are disappointed in their leader. The likely plot: a confidence vote as to whether our prime minister should continue to lead. If this all sounds a little too familiar, it’s because we’ve been here before.

Not since the days of Jim Bolger has a sitting prime minister been followed so relentlessly by coup rumours. This latest episode follows a gaffe-filled week last week, when National MPs were blindsided by Christopher Luxon’s surprise MMP announcement. It doesn’t help that polling continues to show uninspiring numbers for National. 

Now, less than three months out from the election, National MPs are about to head into an urgent caucus meeting in Wellington, called by Luxon after dissatisfaction within National was reported by the NZ Herald on Monday night. It’s the third times coup rumours have swirled around the prime minister since late 2025.

Political commentator Jacqui van der Kaay thinks the question at the front of their minds as they go into the 9.30am meeting will be: “Is the risk of keeping him here greater than the risk of changing now?” On the one hand, she says, they have the opportunity to “energise voters” by forming a new united front around a fresh leader. On the other hand, they will know that you can never really predict how the electorate will react to a new leader. “Voters might also not like [a change], because you’re not showing clear leadership by unseating a sitting prime minister a few months before the election.”

Whatever they decide, Van der Kaay says, being in this position will be “frustrating” for the party, given it is happening because of Luxon’s unclear messaging, gaffes and apologies. The party also needs to consider how coalition partners Act and NZ First would react to a new leader, she says. “The reality is, if it’s going to happen, it has to happen soon. You either need to call it, or say this is it: he’s taking us to the election.”

Claudette Hauiti, a former National MP and political reporter says the right time to roll Luxon was yesterday. Hauiti served as an MP for a year in the 2013/14 Key government, and says that era of the National Party was led by a prime minister who “listened to his troops and his advisors”. The difference with this National caucus is that “Christopher Luxon is a leader that listens to no one,” she says. “I’d get rid of him now, but it comes down to who’s willing to put their hand up. Are they a good leader, and does the caucus have enough balls to back a new leader?”

Holly Bennett, the managing director of government relations firm Awhi, says the real question for the National caucus is whether they are “happy with less than stellar [polling] results” which would only see them “hobble through” to a second term in power. She says that current polling suggests the party won’t go into the election with full confidence “in any way, shape or form”.

Bennett warns that it’s not just the party who will be struggling with Luxon’s performance – traditional National voters would have been “really disappointed” to hear him “talk about business leaders with almost disdain” at a now infamous event in Rotorua 12 days ago. “When I look at some of their most recent policies, they’re not the National Party policies that I’ve come to know,” Bennett says. “Compulsory KiwiSaver is something that troubles me no end, because compulsion is never something the National Party has done.”

Bennett believes National should roll Luxon and replace him with a leader who could “stand up for” the party’s “fundamental values” in the future. She says the sooner they do it, the better.

David Cormack, a public relations expert and former Green Party staffer, disagrees. Change the leadership and you risk rocking the coalition, he says. If NZ First leader Winston Peters “pulls the pin” on the coalition “that would take a whole lot of oxygen” away from a new leader who may never become prime minister. National is likely still scarred by the “English-Bridges-Muller-Collins disaster”, Cormack says (throwing back to the party’s nightmare years of fast-changing leadership before Luxon stepped in) and worried that “any kind of change is going to relitigate” that era.

There will be tension between those on the backbenches whose jobs are on the line at current polling, and those within the kitchen cabinet with safer futures. “The backbenchers have been agitating for quite some time, because a number of them are going, ‘fuck, I’m going to lose my job and this guy sucks’,” Cormack says. His take on the frontbenchers’ feelings? “My job’s alright, but this guy sucks.”

Cormack says if the party plans to roll Luxon it better have a good replacement who will appeal to the public. Commentators are focused on Erica Stanford and Chris Bishop, but Nicola Willis, Chris Penk, Mark Mitchell and Simeon Brown have also been mentioned in the mix. Cormack’s pick? Stanford. She has a few things going for her, he says. She’s Auckland-based, so will be seen as in touch with the country’s largest city, liberal and a woman. At the 2023 election, the typical swing voter was a middle-aged Pākehā woman, and they may respond to Stanford, he thinks. 

For the next few hours at least, Luxon remains the leader. After that? Well, stay tuned.

articles.title: The last time a New Zealand prime minister was booted by their own party
articles.description:
We’re going to need to travel back nearly three decades.

They love a spill in Australia. Four prime ministers have been rolled by their own MPs since 2010. The UK is even hungrier for its own, with four PMs victim of an internal coup in just the last seven years.

New Zealand is a bit different. You have to wind back to the last millennium to find a prime minister removed against their will. It was the last breath of 1997 and the unfortunate victim was Jim Bolger. 

That is a long way back, but not distant enough to defy the great constant of MMP in New Zealand. Winston Peters. He was there in 1997, and furious at Jenny Shipley’s intricately plotted removal of the man with whom he had formed New Zealand’s first coalition under the new electoral system. And he is there in 2026, though you wouldn’t expect him to go into bat for Christopher Luxon, a man for whom Peters has open contempt. We’ll come back to all that in a bit.

Bolger embattled

It’s easy to forget when you consider the waves of affection across his final years and upon his death, but Jim Bolger was not a popular prime minister. Barely had he arrived on the ninth floor of the Beehive in 1990 before he was in the single figures as preferred prime minister, well below Luxon’s ratings.

Bolger battled through, however, and won re-election by a whisker in 1993. In 1996, he negotiated an MMP government with Winston Peters, leader of what Bolger had called “the racist party”, New Zealand First. 

In short order the first MMP government was weighed down by boxer short scandals and economic malaise. The newly installed treasurer, Winston Peters, was scrapping in the house and turning off voters. Bolger, gamely, pronounced it “springtime for New Zealand”, but it didn’t help much. The mood at home was grim as he headed for Europe and a Commonwealth heads of government meeting. 

Jenny Shipley, a formidable senior minister in Bolger governments, was the name most mentioned as a potential replacement for the prime minister. A newspaper profile in 1997 called her the “lady in waiting”. Bolger had asked her to make a public statement that she wouldn’t challenge before the end of the term. 

“I remember saying to him, Jim, you know, neither you or I can predetermine what the caucus will wish to do,” Shipley told The Spinoff in an interview for the Juggernaut podcast. At that point she hadn’t decided to take him on, she said, and she pledged simply to work hard for the government. “It was a real conversation that Jim and I had, and it wasn’t acrimonious. He was probably disappointed that I didn’t say yes, but he couldn’t fault me. I worked hard for that man and our team absolutely every day.”

The Te Puke Bypass 

Before long, though, she had agreed with colleagues that they needed to act. They ran their planning meetings as “the Te Puke Bypass Committee”, a name settled on by her senior private secretary as perfect for exciting precisely zero interest. 

Bolger departed for Europe in late 1997 without any inkling of the plotting under way. His chief of staff, Rob Eaddy, was similarly unaware back at parliament, until he bumped into Roger Sowry, a National cabinet minister, at Bellamy’s restaurant. 

He harmlessly jostled his old friend. “I said, ‘What are you up to, Sowry? You’re bloody plotting again, you little bastard!’ And he gave me a really strange response. He said: ‘You know, Rob, I’ve always told you that I support Jim, but when the time comes to change, I will support that change.’ Then he walked off.”

Shipley had determined that “the kindest way and the most effective way and the least disruptive way was to simply send a pledge letter to my colleagues who I knew supported change… And by using that process over several days, I had a group of pledge letters signed in my possession that had… a comfortable majority of the caucus”.

The task of sharing the news with Bolger was given to Doug Graham, one of Bolger’s great allies, someone, he later told me, who was not “party to all this skullduggery and the backstabbing and number counting”. 

He welcomed Bolger off the plane at Auckland airport. “And I said, look, I think the numbers are against you.”

“And I recall going to my office,” said Bolger, “and I rang up Jenny Shipley’s office and we had a chat, and she was absolutely confident she had the numbers”.

Shipley: “I said to him, look, we can do this the easy way, or we can do this the hard way, but here’s the numbers. And they did test it, they rang a few people, and the rest is history.”

Bolger: “I thought, if that’s what they do when I’m out of the country, then to hell with it, is about time I resigned.”

He was gracious in public. “I leave the office not bitter,” said Bolger. “Bitterness is an extraordinarily destructive emotion, and I refuse to entertain it. I leave it with a sense of great satisfaction for what we’ve been able to achieve together in the seven years I’ve been prime minister. I leave it with enormous hope for the future of the country.”

Shipley became New Zealand’s first female prime minister, but there was little time to celebrate. Among the challenges she confronted was an inflamed Winston Peters. Within a year, she had sacked him from cabinet after an acrimonious spat over the sale of Wellington airport shares. The public judged both poorly, but it did send a message decades into the future. I’ve been told by a well-placed source that as part of preparation for a previous, aborted move against Luxon, a challenger from within cabinet asked of Winston Peters how he would like to be informed about any imminent caucus coup. 

Look back in fondness

At the end of last year, at an event to mark the launch of the second season of Juggernaut at the Embassy in Wellington, National minister Chris Bishop agreed with the proposition that politicians – Jim Bolger as exemplar – tend to grow in popularity after they leave office.

“Look, people finish up their time in politics, and what tends to happen is people remember the good times and they forget the bad times. The country does. And that’s true of most leaders,” he said. 

It’s true, even for those who fell well short of a term – Geoffrey Palmer, say, or Mike Moore. “I think that people have a bit of an optimism bias,” said Bishop. “They do tend to look back more fondly than they did at the time.” That might not be the worst message to mutter into Christopher Luxon’s ear today.

articles.title: Groundhog Day: Christopher Luxon calls a meeting about his leadership – again
articles.description:
In the wake of a week of gaffes, the prime minister’s hold on the National leadership is again looking shaky. Here’s what you need to know.

It’s happening… again. Christopher Luxon has called an urgent caucus meeting for tomorrow at 9.30am to address “increased speculation about my leadership”. 

It’s a recess week and the caucus only had plans to meet online, but the prime minister announced this afternoon that he wants an in-person meeting to “resolve the issue”. 

Call us limited in our thinking, but there’s not a whole lot of ways the caucus can resolve speculation about his leadership. In fact, we’re counting only two: they will back him, or – with less than three months until election day – they will ditch him.

How could this be happening at such an important time in the election cycle, and why does it feel so familiar? Good questions. Let’s dive in.

You can blame Thomas Coughlan, the NZ Herald’s political editor. Last night, he reported that National Party MPs had hit the phones to discuss a potential leadership change. 

Coughlan reported one MP as saying “there’s going to be change” in the top job.

“It’s just a question of who is going to be it.”

Cue a morning of intense speculation and uncomfortable questions.

Of course, we could also look beyond Mr Coughlan for answers. In these Trumpian times, that may seem like a renegade move, but some would argue that Christopher Luxon has had a role – a lead one, even – in what’s going down. 

What’s Luxon done?

He spent a week stumbling from disaster to disaster. It started on Friday, July 31, during a Rotorua Business Chamber event. Luxon was asked: “How long can we hold on?” Now, keep in mind that he was talking to a group of businesspeople who have been doing it tough as New Zealand’s economy has struggled for years. He responded “I think that’s a negative view, to be honest”, then went on to talk about how New Zealand businesses had a “parent-child mentality” in terms of their relationship with the government, and how businesses should be using the AI tool Claude. Three days later he apologised. 

On August 6, he announced that if he was prime minister for another term, he would hold a referendum on MMP. The announcement seemed unplanned, coming during a stint in the studio at ZB with host Kerre Woodham. A listener texted in and he responded with the surprising commitment. This caught his own MPs off guard, who were left floundering – and telling slightly different stories – when asked about the announcement. It also buried a good news story – transport minister Chris Bishop and Auckland mayor Wayne Brown had just announced an opening date for the long-awaited City Rail Link.

Toby Manhire and Veronica Schmidt discuss Luxon on the brink, the countdown to an emergency caucus and the coup chat along the way in a new episode of At Large with Toby Manhire. Available on all the usual platforms including Apple, Spotify, and YouTube.

So, he had a bad week. Is that it?

Not really. Luxon’s communication style has long come in for criticism. His MMP proclamation, for example, has been likened to a seemingly bungled announcement in late July, where he said he would not work with the rising Opportunity Party.

The line in the sand was less the issue as much as how he delivered it. Luxon made that announcement, seemingly off the bat, at the end of a press conference and then walked off as reporters tried to get him to confirm that he’d ruled Opportunity out. His office had to confirm it later. 

Recent gaffes aside, Luxon is deeply unpopular for a first-term prime minister, with his approval rating in the last Taxpayers’ Union/Curia at -19%, well below Labour leader Christopher Hipkins’ of -7%. 

Why does it feel like Groundhog Day?

We have been here before, not once, but twice. This is the third time that the death knell has rung out in Wellington.

Last November, there was speculation, culminating in a piece by The Post journalist Andrea Vance, that Chris Bishop was after the party’s leadership. Bishop denied he was plotting to roll Luxon, but that didn’t stop comparisons between the two Christophers, in which Luxon was often found wanting.

In April, it was all on again. This time the death knell rang so loudly that Luxon called a confidence vote in himself. He emerged, if not unscathed, at least still the leader.

Now, here we are again.

If he goes, who would be National’s next leader?

Talk to any fine political mind and they’ll tell you Bishop’s name is still being mentioned, but also to watch out for Erica Stanford (her statement last week that she wasn’t after the leadership already feels like ancient history). But it could be possible that Nicola Willis, Mark Mitchell and Simeon Brown are in the running.

So, what happens tomorrow? 

The caucus will meet in Wellington tomorrow at 9.30am. What will happen in that meeting? Place your bets …

articles.title: ‘It’s clearly not going to happen’: Labour finally officially rules out working with NZ First
articles.description:
Chris Hipkins has ruled out working with New Zealand First in any government he leads, ending months of hedging on the question, writes Henry Oliver in today’s excerpt from The Bulletin.

To receive The Bulletin in full each weekday, sign up here.

Labour leader Chris Hipkins has officially ruled out working with New Zealand First in any government he leads, ending months of hedging on the question, as reported by RNZ. Speaking yesterday afternoon, Hipkins said simply: “Winston Peters has ruled us out. I’m happy to rule him out. It’s clearly not going to happen.”

Asked why he hadn’t said so sooner, Hipkins pointed to what he called an escalating “pattern of behaviour” from Peters and NZ First, saying he wouldn’t tolerate “overt racism” in any government he led and that not a single member of his caucus had disagreed when the rule-out was discussed. Peters was characteristically unimpressed, posting on X that Hipkins had “severe learning difficulties” and pointing out NZ First had ruled Labour out repeatedly over the past year.

Thomas Coughlan and Julia Gabel at the Herald confirmed the rule-out had been discussed at Labour’s caucus meeting the week before, with no dissent, and noted Hipkins framed the decision explicitly around Peters’ conduct rather than any broader policy disagreement. The move formally closes off one of the coalition permutations that had persisted, at least theoretically, as a live question through much of the year – even as both leaders had spent months publicly ruling each other out anyway.

The preceding partial rule-out

The full rule-out builds on Hipkins comments last week, ruling out any Labour-led government letting Peters continue as foreign affairs minister, also reported by RNZ, following Peters telling Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan to “go back to your own country” in parliament. Hipkins said the comments made Peters’ position “completely untenable,” as he could no longer credibly represent New Zealand internationally.

At the time, Hipkins stopped short of ruling out NZ First altogether, saying only that nothing had changed since the party was excluded ahead of the last election. Peters fired back that he’d already ruled out working with Labour twelve months earlier, and mocked the “low IQ media” for treating Hipkins’ comments as news.

‘Minimum viable opposition’

The announcement came during an underwhelming week for Labour. The Post reported the party’s MPs appeared unrattled by a recent bruising poll result, even as Hipkins dismissed the figures as a “rogue” outlier and pointed to what he said was a steadier upward trend across other public polling.

But Joel MacManus, surveying several of the country’s top campaign strategists on The Spinoff this morning, suggested the calm might be harder to sustain than it looks. Despite weeks of bad headlines for the government – Peters’ comments, Luxon’s Rotorua apology, unemployment hitting an 11-year high – Labour’s numbers haven’t moved, with two polls last week showing National still comfortably ahead and the current coalition parties retaining the numbers to govern.

Strategists described Labour’s approach as a “minimum viable opposition” or “small target” strategy, deliberately avoiding controversy and big policy swings to stay credible without becoming the story. Some argued that discipline had genuinely outperformed expectations given where the party started the term. Others felt the strategy had run its course, arguing Labour needed bolder, more distinctive policy to actually convert disaffected voters – particularly those drifting to the surging Opportunity party – rather than simply waiting for the government’s mistakes to do the work.

articles.title: ‘Minimum viable opposition’: Is Labour’s election strategy backfiring?
articles.description:
Despite weeks of bad headlines for the government, Labour’s poll numbers don’t seem to be improving. What’s going on?

The government has had a bad couple of weeks. The foreign minister offended the Chinese ambassador. The prime minister offended small business owners in Rotorua. And the economic indicators keep getting worse, with the unemployment rate rising to an 11-year high of 5.6%. Many in Labour hoped this might be a turning point.

It came after two months where Labour topped National in seven out of eight public polls, and where the rise of Opportunity has presented a new potential pathway to victory for the left bloc. And yet, the two polls released last week showed no sign of things turning around for the centre-left party: A Roy Morgan poll had National 6.6 ahead, while a Taxpayers’ Union-Curia poll had them 3.2 points ahead. Both showed the three current coalition parties would comfortably have the numbers to govern again. 

The Spinoff spoke with some of New Zealand’s top campaign strategists and political insiders about the state of Labour’s election plans and whether these latest polls showed it was time for a change of strategy. 

Georgina Stylianou, a director of government relations firm BRG, said Labour’s strategy “seems to be controlled visibility, or a minimum viable opposition. They’re doing enough to be credible but not so much that it risks the election becoming a referendum on them before voters finish judging the government”.

Neale Jones, the director of public affairs firm Capital and a former chief of staff to Jacinda Ardern and Andrew Little, said the party had so far aimed to avoid “culture wars and other distractions” and limit expensive or controversial policies. “They’ve rightly identified tax as a risk which is why they did a limited CGT and got it out early and have ruled out other parties’ tax policies,” he said. 

Brigitte Morten, a director of law firm Franks Ogilvie and former National government advisor, compared it to the “small target” strategies of the UK Labour party under Keir Starmer and Australian Labor under Anthony Albanese. “They’ve been focusing on not attracting attention,” she said. “They’ve announced small policies like free GP visits but nothing to demonstrate what they’d do differently. They’ve done that deliberately to avoid scrutiny, and are relying on winning disaffected voters by default.”

However, she argued the MMP environment changed the equation. “This year, the minor parties are making up a much bigger party vote than ever before. The problem for Labour is the Opportunity party vote is mostly coming from Labour and the Greens. Hipkins needs to acknowledge there are other options out there, and right now he’s struggling to make that pitch.”

“We live in an attention economy,” Jones added. “The minor parties hog the headlines. Labour has to show it can be a credible government and not blow the money and be responsible, while also promising that people’s lives will change. That’s a difficult tension to manage.”

Jones and Stylianou said aspects of the strategy had served Labour well so far and the party was in a better position than would have been expected three years ago. “If you’d asked me in 2023 where Labour would be right now, I’d have guessed they’d be polling around 25% and on their third leader of the term,” Jones said. 

“You’ve got to give credit to Hipkins,” Stylianou said. “He’s managed to keep the leadership without any rumours swirling. The media focus has been on National’s leadership not Labour’s. He’s lifted Labour from their abysmal results in 2023, and he’s running a pretty disciplined ship where the MPs all seem united”. 

Morten acknowledged that the small target strategy had helped Labour to outperform its fundamentals. “People still connect Hipkins with a government that spent billions and didn’t deliver. The memory isn’t that old. They’re still the same group of people who did those things. It’s hard for the opposition to make an argument that they’re different from three years ago when it’s literally the same people.”

However, she felt the strategy had run its course. “I think they’re executing, but I think the strategy doesn’t work anymore. They’re getting the result that they need. They’re not really getting the hits on the government that you might see from a strong opposition.”

Stylianou believed there was an active debate among Labour insiders between those who want to continue the small target strategy and those who want to “go bigger, go bolder and roll out more policies”. She described Labour’s existing suite of policies, such as free GP visits and discounted public transport fares, as “tangible little droplets – they’re all good retail policies but they don’t have an overarching pitch.” Though, she added “if you’re someone who is genuinely battling, you can’t write them off”.

If Labour were to make a big splash in a particular policy area, she suggested it should be in the energy sector. “It has all the ingredients for Labour – cost of living, climate, national security, resilience. So I’m looking there and expecting something pretty bold and transformative.” 

Morten also felt Labour needed to take some bigger swings policy-wise. “If they’re going to take soft National or Opportunity votes they’re going to have to be bolder with policies. They have to go out and say what they’re going to do and get people to actively vote for them. People have to want to vote for them”.

“I personally think there’s more opportunity for Labour to be economically populist,” Jones added. “I think there is a mood of genuine anger and frustration at the economic system we have. But Labour has to build a coalition of 50%. It needs to win people over who might have voted for National, they might be doing OK and are scared of change. So Labour always has to look both ways, which makes it far more constrained.”

Labour enters this election campaign with a considerably smaller war chest than National, which may have added to the perception that the party has been less visible – though Morten noted that visibility has become harder to gauge. “One of the joys of an algorithm-driven election campaign is that things are targeted to you. People say ‘I see nothing from National’ or ‘I see nothing from Labour’, but those ads just aren’t being targeted to them.”

Now that we have entered the regulated campaign period, Jones, Morten and Stylianou expected Labour – and especially Hipkins – to be more present on the airwaves. “The very nature of a campaign is that it becomes more presidential,” Jones said. 

Stylianou thought the presidential-style campaign between the two major party leaders would suit Hipkins. “Politics is hearts and minds and that applies to whatever part of the spectrum you’re on. While people might like Luxon’s policies, he’s always had a problem on likability. Hipkins has that quality to him, and I expect we’ll see him leaning into that,” she said. 

She thought it would be a mistake for Labour to try to recreate the same energetic campaign style that worked under Jacinda Ardern. “Hipkins trying to emulate that would be dumb,” she said. “I remember working on a Bill English campaign [in 2017] and it felt like they rolled out a John Key campaign and it wasn’t the right fit for him. It’s the same thing here – Hipkins is his own bloke and should do politics the right way for him, not try to do Jacindamania.”

However, Morten felt Labour needed to find some way to recapture the energy of the Ardern years in order to ensure its base, particularly Pasifika voters in south Auckland, showed up to the polls. “Jacinda Ardern had the ability to capture the imaginations and emotions of voters, and that’s one of the things Labour struggles with now. So that’s a major risk: can they turn out their people?”

articles.title: Bus driver averted catastrophic drone attack at major German airport
articles.description:
BERLIN, Germany: A bus driver at a major German airport stopped a possible attack by knocking a drone carrying explosives out of the air, according to a senior lawmaker.

The incident happened this week at Leipzig/Halle Airport, an important hub for NATO operations and cargo transport. The driver saw the drone flying low while he was working and reacted quickly, striking it and forcing it to crash nearby.

Officials later said the drone was fitted with professional-grade explosives and a detonator. Prosecutors have started a counterterrorism investigation, calling it a serious incident that could have threatened both national and international security.

Authorities have not revealed the identity of the driver. They also have not explained where the drone originated or how it entered a restricted area of the airport.

Leipzig/Halle Airport plays a key role in NATO missions. It serves as the main base for the Strategic Airlift International Solution (SALIS), which uses large Antonov cargo planes to transport military equipment, especially to support NATO's eastern regions. The airport is also widely used by logistics companies such as DHL.

German officials have previously accused Russia of carrying out so-called hybrid attacks, which are aggressive acts that fall short of open warfare. Moscow has denied such claims, and its embassy in Berlin did not comment on this incident.

Media reports said the drone was found near several Ukrainian Antonov An-124 cargo planes, among the largest of their kind. A journalist at the scene saw police gathering evidence near one of the planes on August 5.

Detlef Seif, a lawmaker from the ruling CDU party, described the driver's actions and said, "The bus driver's action was very daring and courageous, but also very dangerous. It is possible that his intervention prevented the intended attack."

Local officials praised the driver's bravery but also warned that people should not try to handle such situations themselves. Saxony's interior minister said reporting the danger would have been enough.

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz discussed the incident with senior ministers and remained in close contact with the interior ministry as authorities continued their investigation.
